# Segmented Validation {#sec-segmented-validation}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```

A single result for the whole table can hide important detail. A check that fails on 2 percent of
rows might be failing evenly across the table, or it might be failing on a quarter of the rows in
one region and nowhere else. Those are very different situations, and you would respond to them
differently. Segmented validation shows you which one you have by running a check separately for
each group in the data and reporting a result for each group.

To segment a check, add the `segments=` argument to it. Most checks that look at individual values
or rows support it. With `segments=`, one step in your plan becomes one step per segment, each with its own counts and its own
pass or fail result. This chapter covers the different ways to define segments: a column name, a
column with a chosen set of values, and `seg_group()` for combining several values into one segment.
It then covers segmenting on several columns at once, how thresholds work with segments, and which
checks support segmentation. We use `game_revenue` throughout, since its `item_type` and
`acquisition` columns give us natural groups.

```{python}
game_revenue = pb.load_dataset(dataset="game_revenue", tbl_type="polars")
```

We start with the simplest form, which splits a check by the values of one column.

## Segmenting by a column

Suppose we want to flag unusually large transactions, on the idea that any single item earning 100
or more is worth a look. Run against the whole table, the check finds only a few failures.


## Choosing which segments to create

Segmenting on a column with many distinct values creates a step for every one of them, which is not
always what you want. If only a few groups interest you, you can pass a tuple to `segments=` with
the column name and a list of the values you want. Here we check only the `organic` and `apple`
acquisition channels.


## Combining values into one segment with `seg_group`

Sometimes you want to treat several values as one group, such as a set of acquisition channels that
are all unpaid. The `seg_group()` helper combines a list of values into a single segment, so the
check runs once across all of them instead of once per value. Here we group the `organic` and
`facebook` channels.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_gt(
        columns="item_revenue", value=0,
        segments=("acquisition", pb.seg_group(["organic", "facebook"])),
    )
    .interrogate()
)
```

The result is one step covering 1,206 rows (1,038 organic plus 168 facebook), rather than two
separate steps. If you pass a list of lists to `seg_group()`, you get several combined segments at
once. For example, `pb.seg_group([["organic", "facebook"], ["google", "apple"]])` produces two
steps, one with 1,206 rows and one with 413. All the values in a group must be the same type. Mixing
a string and a number in one group raises a `TypeError`.

## Segmenting across several columns

So far we have segmented on one column at a time. You can also pass a list of column names to
`segments=`, which segments on each column separately within the same step. This is not a
cross-product of the columns. Each column gets its own set of segments.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_lt(columns="item_revenue", value=100, segments=["item_type", "acquisition"])
    .interrogate()
)
```

The one step becomes eight: two for the `item_type` values and six for the `acquisition` channels.
The `item_type` segments show the same result as before, with all six failures in `iap`. The
`acquisition` segments show the same six failures spread over three channels: four in `organic`,
one in `google`, and one in `other_campaign`. So the large purchases are not coming from one
particular channel. If you want every combination of item type and channel, Pointblank does not
create that for you. Instead, you can add a column that combines the two and segment on that.

Because one step can turn into many, be careful about which columns you segment on. Segmenting on a
column with thousands of distinct values, like an ID column, produces thousands of steps and a
report nobody can read, so stick to columns with a manageable number of groups. Also check that the
values you name actually occur in the data. If you name a value that is not there, Pointblank still
creates a step for it, and that step covers zero rows and shows an evaluation error in the report.

## How segments interact with thresholds

Each segment is a full validation step, so thresholds apply to each segment on its own rather than
to the check as a whole. This is often the main reason to segment. A failure rate that looks fine
across the whole table can be much higher within one group. Our revenue check has 6 failures out of
2,000 rows, a rate of 0.003, which is well under a warning threshold of 0.01.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue, thresholds=pb.Thresholds(warning=0.01))
    .col_vals_lt(columns="item_revenue", value=100)
    .interrogate()
)
```

The step does not reach the warning level, since 0.003 is below 0.01, so this plan would not raise a
warning. Now let's segment the same check by `item_type` with the same threshold.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue, thresholds=pb.Thresholds(warning=0.01))
    .col_vals_lt(columns="item_revenue", value=100, segments="item_type")
    .interrogate()
)
```

The `ad` segment still passes. The `iap` segment has the same six failures, but now out of 447 rows
instead of 2,000, which is a rate of about 0.013. That is above 0.01, so the segment is marked at the
warning level. The same six rows that were an acceptable rate for the whole table now trigger a
warning, because they are measured against the group they belong to. This is how segmented
thresholds catch a problem that is serious within one group but rare across the table.

## Where segmentation applies

Segmentation works with checks that evaluate the data row by row, which is most of them. Nearly
all of the `col_vals_*` methods accept `segments=` (the exception is `col_vals_in_table()`). So do
`rows_distinct()` and `rows_complete()` from @sec-row-validations, the three row-level
missing-value methods from @sec-missing-data, and `prompt()` from @sec-semantic-validation. All of
these produce a result for each row, which is what makes it possible to split the rows into groups.
